Καί φησιν· «Οὗτος κεῖται εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν ἐν τῷ
Ἰσραὴλ καὶ εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον», «εἰς πτῶσιν» τῶν ἐπιμενόντων τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ,

«εἰς ἀνάστασιν» τῶν ἐξ ἀπιστίας εἰς πίστιν μετατιθεμένων. Λίθος ἦν ὁ Χριστὸς εἰς
οἰκοδομὴν κείμενος, ἀλλὰ προσέκοπτον οἱ τυφλοὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ῥεμβόμενοι. Οὐ
τοίνυν αὐτῷ τὴν «πτῶσιν» τῶν πεπτω-κότων, ἀλλὰ τὴν «ἀνάστασιν» λογίζεσθαι
χρή. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἔπιπτον μόνον, οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ ἀνίσταντο, δικαίως αὐτὸν τῆς «πτώσεως»
ὑποπτεύεις αἴτιον. Εἰ δὲ τῶν ἐκ ῥαθυμίας πιπτόντων οἱ βουληθέντες ἀνίστανται, τὸ
«πτῶμα» τοῦ ῥαθυμοῦντος γίνεται, τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἡ «ἀνάστασις». Οὐκ ἔπεσον Ἰούδας
ἅμα καὶ Πέτρος, ὁ μὲν ὡς εἰπών· «Τί μοι θέλετε δοῦναι, κἀγὼ ὑμῖν παραδώσω
αὐτόν;» ὁ δὲ ὡς εἰπών· «Τὴν ψυχήν μου ὑπὲρ σοῦ θήσω»; Ἐχρῆν γὰρ αὐτὸν εἰδέναι
ὅτι θνητὸς τὴν ψυχὴν ὑπὲρ ἀθανασίας οὐ δίδωσι. Καὶ πάλιν· «Ἐὰν δέῃ με σὺν σοὶ
3
ἀποθανεῖν, οὐ μή σε ἀπαρνήσομαι.» Ἐξὸν εἰπεῖν· «Ἐάν με ἐνισχύσῃς, οὐ μή σε
ἀπαρνήσομαι. Ἐὰν ἀσφαλίσῃ με, ὁ ἀσθενὴς οὐ δέδοικα τὸ ναυάγιον. Ἐὰν τῷ πολέμῳ
κοινωνήσῃς, οὐκ εὐλαβοῦμαι θάνατον.» Ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν γλώττης ὑπῆρχεν, τὸ δὲ
καρδίας ἁμάρτημα. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο <ὁ> μὲν Πέτρος πεσὼν ἀνέστη καὶ χειραγωγὸς ἑτέρων
πεπτωκότων ἐγένετο· ὁ δέ, ἀπὸ βάθους πρὸς βόθρον ὁδηγηθείς, ἔρριψε τὸ ἀργύριον
καὶ τὸ σχοινίον λαβὼν ἀπήγξατο.
8 «Σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον» ὁ σταυρός· τῶν γὰρ Ἰουδαίων σταυρούντων,
ἀνεχώρει ὁ ἥλιος· ἡ συναγωγὴ ἐσυκοφάντει καὶ ἡ γῆ ἐσαλεύετο. Ὁ λαὸς ἐβόα·
«Σταύρωσον αὐτόν», ἀλλ' αἱ πέτραι μὴ φέρουσαι τὸν ὄγκον τῆς βλασφημίας
ἐρρήγνυντο. Οἱ πρεσβύτεροι καὶ οἱ γραμματεῖς ἔλεγον· «Ἐμνήσθημεν ὅτι ὁ πλάνος
ἐκεῖνος εἶπεν ἔτι ζῶν ὅτι μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἐγείρομαι.» Ὁ δὲ ἑκατόνταρχος ἐβόα·
«Ἀληθῶς θεοῦ υἱὸς ἦν οὗτος.» Ἀλλὰ καὶ μέχρι νῦν ὁ λόγος ὁ τοῦ σταυροῦ
«Ἰουδαίοις μὲν σκάνδαλον, ἔθνεσι δὲ μωρία, ἡμῖν δὲ τοῖς κλητοῖς Χριστὸς θεοῦ
δύναμις καὶ θεοῦ σοφία.» «Καὶ σοῦ δὲ αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διελεύσεται ῥομφαία, ὅπως
ἂν ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν ἐκ πολλῶν καρδιῶν διαλογισμοί.» Ῥομφαία ἡ διχόνοια λέγεται
ἐπειδὴ, καθάπερ ἡ ῥομφαία σχίζει καὶ μερίζει τὰ σώματα, οὕτως καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς πρὸς
ἀμφιβολὴν ἡ διχόνοια· εἰ γὰρ καὶ παρθένος ἦν, ἀλλὰ καὶ γυνή· εἰ καὶ θεοτόκος, ἀλλ'
ἐκ τοῦ ἡμετέρου φυράματος. Ῥομφαία τοίνυν αὐτῆς τὴν ψυχὴν διέβαινεν, «ὅπως
<ἂν> ἀποκαλυφθῶσιν ἐκ πολλῶν καρδιῶν διαλογισμοί.» Ποῖοι διαλογισμοί; Οἱ περὶ
τοῦ Χριστοῦ κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦ πάθους διάφοροι, ποτὲ μὲν αὐτὸν προφήτην, ποτὲ
δὲ λυτρωτὴν τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ οὐχ ὑπογράφοντες, πολλὴν καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις ἀμφιβολίαν διὰ
τὸν σάλον τὸν ἐκ τοῦ πάθους ὑπομένοντες, ὥστε τοὺς περὶ Κλεόπαν μαθητὰς
παριόντας καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν λέγειν· «Σὺ μόνος παροικεῖς ἐν Ἰερουσαλὴμ καὶ οὐκ
ἔγνως τὰ γενόμενα ἐν αὐτῇ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέ ραις ταύταις.» Εἶτα ἐρωτηθέντες «ποῖα;»
ἐπήγαγον· «Τὰ περὶ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ Ναζωραίου, ὃς ἐγένετο ἀνὴρ προφήτης, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς.»
Οὐκοῦν ὥσπερ προφήτην μὲν εἶχον καὶ λυτρούμενον τὸν Ἰσραήλ· διὰ δὲ τὸ πάθος
καὶ ταύτην ἐμβάλλειν περὶ αὐτοῦ τὴν ὑπόληψιν ὅτι λυτροῦται τὸν Ἰσραὴλ
ἐκινδύνευον. Τοῦτο δὲ οὐ μάτην ἐγίνετο, ἀλλ' ὥστε δεῖξαι ὅτι «τὸ μωρὸν τοῦ θεοῦ
σοφώτερον τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐστίν.» Τὸ γὰρ τοῦ σταυροῦ πάθος οἱ πάντες
ἐσινιάσθησαν καὶ ἐσαλεύθησαν, οὐ μόνον οἱ ἁπλῶς μαθηταί, ἀλλὰ καὶ οἱ ἐκλεκτοὶ
καὶ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ. Τοῦτο πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην ἐστήριξεν, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ
κυρίῳ ἡμῶν, δι' οὗ καὶ μεθ' οὗ τῷ Πατρὶ ἡ δόξα, σὺν ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι, νῦν καὶ ἀεὶ καὶ
εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν.

thought_title: The sign of contradiction is the cross
orientation: Hesychius is closing the homily by expounding Simeon's words about the sign of contradiction, interpreting it as the cross and its divisive effect on hearts.
pass_a_gloss: And he says: "This one is set for fall and rising of many in Israel and for a sign of contradiction," "for fall" of those remaining in unbelief, "for rising" of those being transferred from unbelief to faith. Christ was a stone set for building, but the blind, wandering in their eyes, were stumbling. Therefore one must not reckon to him the "fall" of those who have fallen, but the "rising." For if they only fell, and did not also rise, you would rightly suspect him as cause of the "fall." But if of those falling from carelessness the ones who wish rise, the "fall" becomes of the careless one, the "rising" of Christ. Did not Judas and Peter fall together, the one as having said: "What do you want to give me, and I will hand him over to you?" the other as having said: "I will lay down my life for you"? For he ought to have known that a mortal does not give his life for immortality. And again: "If it is necessary for me to die with you, I will never deny you." It was possible to say: "If you strengthen me, I will never deny you. If you secure me, I the weak one do not fear the shipwreck. If you share in the war, I do not shrink from death." But the one was of the tongue, the other a sin of the heart. Therefore Peter, having fallen, rose and became a guide of others who had fallen; but the other, led from depth to pit, threw away the silver and taking the rope hanged himself. "Sign of contradiction" is the cross; for while the Jews were crucifying, the sun withdrew; the synagogue slandered and the earth was shaken. The crowd was shouting: "Crucify him," but the rocks, not bearing the weight of the blasphemy, were split. The elders and the scribes were saying: "We remembered that that deceiver said while still living that after three days I rise." But the centurion was shouting: "Truly this man was son of God." But even until now the word of the cross is "to Jews a scandal, to Gentiles foolishness, but to us who are called Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God." "And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that reasonings from many hearts may be revealed." The sword is called discernment because, just as the sword splits and divides bodies, so also discernment tests souls; for even if she was a virgin, yet also a woman; even if Mother of God, yet from our dough. Therefore a sword was passing through her soul, "so that reasonings from many hearts may be revealed." What reasonings? The various ones about Christ at the time of the passion, sometimes calling him prophet, sometimes redeemer of Israel, enduring much doubt also about these things because of the shaking from the passion, so that the disciples around Cleopas, passing by and saying to him: "Are you the only one dwelling in Jerusalem and did you not know the things that happened in it in these days?" Then being asked "what things?" they added: "The things about Jesus the Nazarene, who became a man prophet, and the rest." Therefore they had him as prophet and as redeeming Israel; but because of the passion they were in danger of casting away also this supposition about him, that he redeems Israel. But this did not happen in vain, but so as to show that "the foolishness of God is wiser than men." For at the passion of the cross all were sifted and shaken, not only the simple disciples, but also the elect and his mother. This established the whole world, in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom to the Father be glory, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term; the homily interprets it as the cross.
Fixed glossary term; used for the fall of those persisting in unbelief.
Fixed glossary term; used for the rising of those turning to faith.
Fixed glossary term; the sword that pierces Mary's soul, interpreted as division.
The homily explicitly equates the sword with διχόνοια, division that leads souls to doubt; rendering as 'division of mind' preserves the psychological sense.
The verb σινιάζω means to sift as wheat; 'were sifted' keeps the agricultural metaphor of testing and shaking.

pass_b_english: And he says: “This child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign of contradiction” (Luke 2:34)—for the fall of those who persist in unbelief, and for the rising of those who turn from unbelief to faith. Christ was a stone set for building, but the blind stumbled as their eyes wandered. So we must not attribute the fall of those who have fallen to him, but rather the rising. For if they only fell and did not also rise, you would rightly suspect him of causing the fall. But if those who fall through carelessness rise when they choose to, then the fall belongs to the careless one, and the rising belongs to Christ. Did Judas and Peter not fall together—the one as having said, “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matthew 26:15), the other as having said, “I will lay down my soul for you” (John 13:37)? For he should have known that a mortal does not give his soul for immortality. And again: “Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you” (Matthew 26:35). He could have said: “If you strengthen me, I will never deny you. If you make me secure, I who am weak do not fear shipwreck. If you share in the battle, I do not shrink from death.” But the one was a matter of the tongue, and the other a sin of the heart. Therefore Peter fell and rose again, and became a guide for others who had fallen; but the other, led from the depths to the pit, threw away the silver, took the rope, and hanged himself.

The sign of contradiction is the cross. For when the Jews crucified him, the sun withdrew; the synagogue slandered him, and the earth shook. The crowd cried out, “Crucify him” (Luke 23:21), but the rocks, unable to bear the weight of the blasphemy, split apart. The elders and the scribes said, “We remember that this deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise’” (Matthew 27:63). But the centurion cried out, “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matthew 27:54). And even to this day the word of the cross is “a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to us who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23-24). “And a sword will pierce your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). The sword is called division of mind, because just as a sword cuts and divides bodies, so division of mind leads souls to doubt. For even if she was a virgin, she was also a woman; even if she was the Mother of God, she was from our own clay. So the sword passed through her soul, “so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). What thoughts? The various thoughts about Christ at the time of the passion—sometimes calling him a prophet, sometimes not acknowledging him as the redeemer of Israel—and enduring great doubt about these things because of the turmoil of the passion. So the disciples with Cleopas came up and said to him, “Are you the only one staying in Jerusalem who does not know what has happened there in these days?” (Luke 24:18). Then, when asked “What things?”, they went on: “The things about Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet,” and so on (Luke 24:19). So they held him as a prophet and as the one who redeems Israel; but because of the passion, they were in danger of casting into doubt even this belief about him, that he redeems Israel. This did not happen in vain, but to show that “the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:25). For at the suffering of the cross, all were perplexed and shaken—not only the ordinary disciples, but also the chosen ones and his mother. This is what established the whole world, in Christ Jesus our Lord, through whom and with whom to the Father be glory, with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

problems.source_quote: Τὴν ψυχήν μου ὑπὲρ σοῦ θήσω
problems.why: The quote is from Matthew 26:35 (or Mark 14:31), not John 13:37. John 13:37 is 'Lord, why can I not follow you now?'
problems.fix: “I will lay down my life for you” (Matthew 26:35)
problems.ruling: Source quotes Matthew 26:35 context; English cites John 13:37, a wrong scripture reference.

edits.new: “I will lay down my life for you” (Matthew 26:35)

problems.quote: The sword is called division of mind
problems.why: The Greek says 'The sword is called division' or 'Division is called sword'. The English 'division of mind' adds 'of mind' which is interpretation. However, 'διχόνοια' does mean 'division, discord, dissension'—literally 'split-mind'. The English is interpretive but within range. No major error.

problems.quote: to the ages of ages
problems.why: Standard doxology. 'To the ages of ages' or 'forever and ever'. No error.

problems.quote: they were in danger of losing even this belief about him, that he redeems Israel
problems.source_quote: καὶ ταύτην ἐμβάλλειν περὶ αὐτοῦ τὴν ὑπόληψιν ὅτι λυτροῦται τὸν Ἰσραὴλ ἐκινδύνευον
problems.why: ἐμβάλλειν means 'to cast/throw into doubt,' not 'losing.' They were in danger of casting this belief into doubt, not losing it.
problems.fix: they were in danger of casting into doubt even this belief about him, that he redeems Israel
problems.ruling: ἐμβάλλειν τὴν ὑπόληψιν means 'cast/throw the belief into doubt,' not 'losing' it; meaning shifted.

problems.quote: all were sifted and shaken
problems.why: ἐσινιάσθησαν means 'were in doubt/perplexed,' not 'sifted.' The word relates to σινία (sieve) but means mental perplexity here.
problems.fix: all were perplexed and shaken
problems.ruling: ἐσινιάσθησαν from σινιάζομαι means 'were sifted/winnowed' metaphorically 'in doubt'; but 'sifted' is literal, misleading without context.

problems.quote: Matthew 26:35
problems.source_quote: Τὴν ψυχήν μου ὑπὲρ σοῦ θήσω
problems.why: Peter's words 'I will lay down my life for you'—checking Matthew 26:35 vs John 13:37. In Matthew 26:35, Peter says 'Ἐὰν δέῃ με σὺν σοὶ ἀποθανεῖν, οὐ μή σε ἀπαρνήσομαι' (Even if I must die with you, I will never deny you). But 'Τὴν ψυχήν μου ὑπὲρ σοῦ θήσω' is from John 13:37. The English cites Matthew 26:35 for both quotes, but the first quote ('I will lay down my life for you') is John 13:37, not Matthew 26:35. This is a wrong scripture citation.
problems.fix: John 13:37
problems.ruling: Source quotes 'Τὴν ψυχήν μου ὑπὲρ σοῦ θήσω' (John 13:37) but English cites Matthew 26:35—wrong reference.

problems.quote: I will lay down my life for you
problems.source_quote: Τὴν ψυχήν μου ὑπὲρ σοῦ θήσω
problems.why: The Greek says 'I will lay down my soul for you' (ψυχήν = soul), not 'life'. While 'life' is a common interpretation, the Greek specifically has 'soul', and the homily immediately discusses this: 'θνητὸς τὴν ψυχὴν ὑπὲρ ἀθανασίας οὐ δίδωσι' (a mortal does not give his soul for immortality). The English 'life' obscures the wordplay between 'soul' in the quote and 'soul' in the commentary. This loses the theological point.
problems.fix: I will lay down my soul for you
problems.ruling: Source 'ψυχήν' = soul; 'life' loses wordplay with 'τὴν ψυχὴν' in commentary, misleading the reader.

problems.quote: a mortal does not give his life for immortality
problems.source_quote: θνητὸς τὴν ψυχὴν ὑπὲρ ἀθανασίας οὐ δίδωσι
problems.why: The Greek has 'ψυχήν' (soul), not 'life'. The English translated the quote as 'life' then continues with 'life' here, missing the connection. The commentary explicitly plays on 'soul' (ψυχήν) from Peter's statement.
problems.fix: a mortal does not give his soul for immortality
problems.ruling: Source 'τὴν ψυχὴν' = soul; 'life' breaks the explicit wordplay linking quote to commentary.

problems.quote: the one was a matter of the tongue, and the other a sin of the heart
problems.source_quote: τὸ μὲν γλώττης ὑπῆρχεν, τὸ δὲ καρδίας ἁμάρτημα
problems.why: The Greek τὸ μέν... τὸ δέ refers to Peter's two statements (the boastful words), not comparing Peter and Judas. The homily says Peter's first statement ('I will lay down my soul') was from tongue, the second ('I will never deny you') was sin of heart. The English makes it sound like Peter vs Judas ('the one... the other'). This misattributes the contrast.
problems.fix: the one was a matter of the tongue, the other a sin of the heart
problems.ruling: Source 'τὸ μὲν...τὸ δὲ' contrasts Peter's two statements, not Peter vs Judas; English 'the one...the other' misleads.

problems.quote: who was a prophet mighty in deed and word
problems.source_quote: ὃς ἐγένετο ἀνὴρ προφήτης, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς
problems.why: The Greek says 'who became/was a man prophet, and so on'. The English adds 'mighty in deed and word' which is not in the Greek 'καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς' (and the following things). This is an addition from Luke 24:19's fuller text, but the Greek here just says 'and so on'. The English expands the quotation beyond what the source gives.
problems.fix: who was a man prophet, and so on
problems.ruling: Source 'καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς' = 'and so on'; English adds 'mighty in deed and word' not in Greek, misleading the reader.

problems.why: The Greek ἀνὴρ προφήτης means "a man, a prophet" or "a prophet mighty in deed and word" (the full Lukan phrase). The English "a man prophet" is ungrammatical and unclear. It should be "a man, a prophet" or "a prophet" or follow Luke's fuller phrase. "Man prophet" is not natural English and obscures that ἀνὴρ here emphasizes he was a human being, a prophet.

problems.quote: The sword is called division of mind
problems.why: Reads like a compressed gloss; 'division of mind' is not a natural English phrase.
problems.fix: Render as 'The sword signifies a divided mind' or 'inner division'.

problems.quote: The sword is called division of mind, because just as a sword cuts and divides bodies, so division of mind leads souls to doubt.
problems.why: 'Division of mind' is awkward; the argument needs 'inner turmoil' or 'mental division'.
problems.fix: Use 'inner turmoil' or 'mental division' for clarity.

dismissed.quote: So they held him as a prophet and as the one who redeems Israel
dismissed.why: The English reverses the construction. Greek says 'they held him as prophet and as redeeming Israel'—the participle λυτρούμενον is active 'redeeming', not 'the one who redeems'. But more importantly, the next clause says 'because of the passion, they were in danger of casting into doubt even this belief about him, that he redeems Israel.' The English 'casting into doubt even this belief' for ἐμβάλλειν... τὴν ὑπόληψιν is slightly off—it's 'putting into doubt' or 'bringing in doubt'. Not major.
dismissed.note: Checker concedes 'not major' and gives no fix; English is accurate.

dismissed.quote: they were in danger of casting into doubt even this belief about him, that he redeems Israel.
dismissed.why: Source says they were in danger of entertaining this belief (that he redeems Israel), not casting it into doubt.
dismissed.note: Context (ἀμφιβολίαν, danger from the passion) requires doubt about the belief they already held; 'entertaining this belief' inverts the logic.
